passage.title: The Tin of Heirloom Seeds
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Late October sunlight slanted through the cedar boards of Grandma Ruth's barn in Macon County, Georgia. The air smelled of dry corn husks and sweet red clay. Ten-year-old Eli sat on an upturned apple crate beside a wide wooden table covered with brown paper sacks. Now that the autumn harvest of 1936 was finished, it was time to save the best vegetable seeds for next spring. Grandma Ruth carried over a painted biscuit tin that had belonged to her own mother fifty years ago.

Inside the tin rested dozens of small cloth pouches tied with white cotton string. Each pouch held heirloom seeds passed down through the family from one season to the next. Grandma Ruth untied a little bag and poured a handful of speckled butterbeans onto a clean china plate. The plumpest bean seeds, dried on the sunny back porch for three full weeks, were carefully sorted by Eli into small paper envelopes. He set aside any wrinkled or cracked beans for the chickens to eat.

At first, Eli wondered why they did not simply buy new seed packets at the general store in town. Sorting every tiny tomato and okra seed by hand made his shoulders ache. Grandma Ruth picked up a large purple hull pea and held it in a patch of golden light. She explained that store seeds often came from distant farms with cool, wet weather. Their family seeds came from plants that had already proved they could survive Georgia's hot July sun.

Every fall, Grandma Ruth picked pods only from the strongest, sweetest vines in the garden row. By saving seeds from the toughest plants year after year, each new crop grew a little hardier than the last. She handed Eli a stubby lead pencil so he could label the next row of folded brown packets. In neat letters, he wrote the name of each crop and the year on the front flap. His handwriting looked just like his grandfather's old notes inside the tin lid.

When the last pouch of yellow squash seeds was tied shut, Grandma Ruth closed the metal lid with a firm click. She placed the tin on the highest shelf where field mice could not reach it during the winter. Eli looked at his ink-stained fingers and felt a quiet pride in the afternoon's slow work. Those tiny dry specks did not look like much on a plate right now. Yet inside that tin waited a whole summer of green vines and full dinner tables.

tier2Words.definition: something valuable, such as a traditional plant variety or family object, passed down through generations
tier2Words.rootHint: From heir ('person who inherits') + loom ('tool or prized possession')
tier2Words.contextClue: Each pouch held seeds passed down through the family from one season to the next in a fifty-year-old tin.

tier2Words.definition: marked with many small spots or patches of color
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old English specca, meaning 'small spot or mark'
tier2Words.contextClue: Grandma Ruth poured the spotted butterbeans onto a clean white china plate so Eli could see them clearly.

tier2Words.definition: to stay alive and keep growing through difficult conditions
tier2Words.contextClue: Their family seeds came from strong plants that could live through Georgia's hot July sun.

tier2Words.definition: stronger and better able to handle tough weather without dying
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old French hardi, meaning 'bold, tough, and sturdy'
tier2Words.contextClue: By saving seeds from the toughest plants year after year, each new crop grew stronger than the last.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The plumpest bean seeds, dried on the sunny back porch for three full weeks, were carefully sorted by Eli into small paper envelopes."

Based on the structure of the sentence, who or what sorted the bean seeds?

options.text: Eli sorted the plumpest bean seeds into small paper envelopes.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'by Eli' right after 'were carefully sorted' shows that ten-year-old Eli is the one who sorted the plumpest bean seeds into small paper envelopes.

options.text: The small paper envelopes sorted Eli on the back porch.
options.childFeedback: This flips the sentence in a silly way! Paper envelopes are just containers that hold the seeds; Eli is the person sorting the beans.

options.text: The sunny back porch sorted the bean seeds for three full weeks.
options.childFeedback: The sunny back porch is only where the bean seeds were dried for three weeks before Eli sorted them into envelopes.

options.text: The plumpest bean seeds sorted themselves into the biscuit tin.
options.childFeedback: Bean seeds cannot sort themselves! In Paragraph 2, the plumpest bean seeds receive the action when Eli sorts them by hand.

questions.provingSentenceText: The plumpest bean seeds, dried on the sunny back porch for three full weeks, were carefully sorted by Eli into small paper envelopes.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'by Eli' right after 'were carefully sorted' shows that ten-year-old Eli is the one who sorted the plumpest bean seeds into small paper envelopes.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'The plumpest bean seeds' receives the action, while 'by Eli' names Eli as the actor who sorted the seeds.
questions.retryHint: Look at the words 'were carefully sorted by Eli' in Paragraph 2 to see who did the sorting.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 4:

"Every fall, Grandma Ruth picked pods only from the strongest, sweetest vines in the garden row. By saving seeds from the toughest plants year after year, each new crop grew a little hardier than the last."

What does the word hardier mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: Smaller and harder to see on a china plate
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 says Eli saved the plumpest bean seeds on the china plate, and 'hardier' describes how strong the growing plants are, not how hard they are to see.

options.text: Sturdier and better able to handle tough conditions
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'hardier' means sturdier and better able to handle tough conditions, because Grandma Ruth saves seeds from the strongest, toughest plants that survived the hot summer.

options.text: More expensive to buy at the town general store
options.childFeedback: Grandma Ruth saves her own family seeds for free instead of buying packets at the general store, so 'hardier' has nothing to do with store prices.

options.text: Softer and easier to crush inside a paper sack
options.childFeedback: Softer and easier to crush is the opposite of 'hardier,' which builds on the clue 'from the toughest plants year after year' in Paragraph 4.

questions.provingSentenceText: By saving seeds from the toughest plants year after year, each new crop grew a little hardier than the last.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'hardier' means sturdier and better able to handle tough conditions, because Grandma Ruth saves seeds from the strongest, toughest plants that survived the hot summer.
questions.parentExplanation: The surrounding context clues ('strongest, sweetest vines' and 'toughest plants') show that 'hardier' means stronger and better able to withstand harsh weather.
questions.retryHint: Look at the clues 'strongest, sweetest vines' and 'toughest plants' in Paragraph 4 to figure out what 'hardier' means.

questions.prompt: According to Paragraph 2, what does Eli do with the bean seeds that are wrinkled or cracked?

options.text: He plants them right away in the red clay behind the barn.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 1, the autumn harvest is just finishing and the saved seeds are for next spring—Eli does not plant cracked beans in October.

options.text: He ties them inside the painted biscuit tin for fifty years.
options.childFeedback: Only the plumpest, healthiest seeds get packed into the fifty-year-old biscuit tin; the wrinkled or cracked beans are separated out.

options.text: He sets them aside so the chickens can eat them.
options.childFeedback: The last sentence of Paragraph 2 states that Eli set aside any wrinkled or cracked beans for the chickens to eat while keeping only the plumpest seeds for next spring.

options.text: He trades them for a new lead pencil at the general store.
options.childFeedback: Grandma Ruth hands Eli a stubby lead pencil in Paragraph 4; he never trades cracked beans at the general store.

questions.provingSentenceText: He set aside any wrinkled or cracked beans for the chickens to eat.
questions.childTip: The last sentence of Paragraph 2 states that Eli set aside any wrinkled or cracked beans for the chickens to eat while keeping only the plumpest seeds for next spring.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 directly states that while Eli sorted the plumpest seeds into envelopes for planting, 'He set aside any wrinkled or cracked beans for the chickens to eat.'
questions.retryHint: Read the very last sentence of Paragraph 2 to see where the wrinkled or cracked beans go.

questions.prompt: How do Paragraphs 3 and 4 change Eli's attitude toward sorting seeds?

options.text: They show why Eli decides to stop helping his grandmother and go into town instead.
options.childFeedback: Eli never quits or goes into town; in Paragraph 4 he carefully labels the seed packets with a pencil just like his grandfather did.

options.text: They describe how a sudden rainstorm ruins the seeds drying on the back porch.
options.childFeedback: No rainstorm happens in the story—the bean seeds had already dried on the sunny back porch for three weeks.

options.text: They prove that field mice have already eaten most of the yellow squash seeds.
options.childFeedback: Field mice are only mentioned in Paragraph 5 when Grandma Ruth puts the closed tin on a high shelf where mice cannot reach it.

options.text: They explain the value of the family's hardy seeds, turning Eli's tiredness into pride.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, Eli starts out tired and wondering why they don't just buy store seeds, but Grandma Ruth's explanation of how their family seeds survive hot summers makes him feel proud by Paragraph 5.

questions.provingSentenceText: Their family seeds came from plants that had already proved they could survive Georgia's hot July sun.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, Eli starts out tired and wondering why they don't just buy store seeds, but Grandma Ruth's explanation of how their family seeds survive hot summers makes him feel proud by Paragraph 5.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 3, Eli starts out with aching shoulders wondering why they don't just buy store packets. Once Grandma Ruth explains in Paragraphs 3–4 how their family seeds are adapted to Georgia's hot sun, Eli feels pride in continuing the family tradition.
questions.retryHint: Compare how Eli feels at the start of Paragraph 3 (when his shoulders ache) with how he feels after learning why their family seeds are special.

questions.prompt: Part A: Why are Grandma Ruth's heirloom seeds better suited for her garden than seeds from the general store?

options.text: They come from plants that have already proved they can handle Georgia's hot summer weather.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that while store seeds often come from distant farms with cool, wet weather, Grandma Ruth's heirloom seeds come from plants that have already proved they can survive Georgia's hot July sun.

options.text: They can grow indoors inside a dark cedar barn without needing any sunlight or water.
options.childFeedback: The seeds are only stored inside the cedar barn for the winter so they can grow into green garden vines outdoors next summer.

options.text: They were grown on distant northern farms where the weather stays cool and wet all year.
options.childFeedback: This mixes up the two types of seeds! Paragraph 3 says the general store seeds are the ones from distant farms with cool, wet weather.

options.text: They are coated in special ink that keeps field mice and chickens away from the garden.
options.childFeedback: Eli gets ink on his fingers while labeling the paper packets, not from coating the seeds, and Grandma Ruth uses a high shelf to keep mice away.

questions.provingSentenceText: Their family seeds came from plants that had already proved they could survive Georgia's hot July sun.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that while store seeds often come from distant farms with cool, wet weather, Grandma Ruth's heirloom seeds come from plants that have already proved they can survive Georgia's hot July sun.
questions.parentExplanation: Grandma Ruth explains in Paragraph 3 that store seeds often come from cool, wet farms far away, whereas their family's heirloom seeds come from plants proven to survive Georgia's hot July sun.
questions.retryHint: Check the last two sentences of Paragraph 3 to see how Grandma Ruth compares store seeds with their own family seeds.
